page_title: A Look into Intel Xeon 6’s Memory Subsystem

sources.entry: A Look into Intel Xeon 6's Memory Subsystem - Measures per-die L3 under sub-NUMA clustering and the die-crossing cost on Granite Rapids beside Turin.

summary.title: A Look into Intel Xeon 6's Memory Subsystem
summary.one_liner: Intel Xeon 6's chiplet layout, SNC3 NUMA mode, L3 and DRAM latency and bandwidth, and cross-die costs, measured on AWS r8i instances and compared with Emerald Rapids and AMD Zen 5 Turin.
keywords: is intel xeon 6 faster than amd epyc memory
takeaways: Xeon 6 6985P-C on AWS r8i uses SNC3 mode (Intel's default), splitting the chip into three NUMA nodes, each backed by its die's DRAM controllers and L3.
Local L3 latency is about 33 ns, but each core can reach a 160 MB L3 pool on its tile; crossing one die boundary adds about 24 ns.
Local DRAM latency is higher than on AMD Turin's NPS1 setup, but remote-die DRAM accesses add about 26 ns per boundary crossed.
Aggregate DRAM bandwidth reached 691.62 GB/s, versus 323.45 GB/s on Emerald Rapids and 478.98 GB/s on EPYC 9355P in unified mode.
Intel's logically monolithic mesh gives a larger, more unified L3 and lower core-to-core latency than AMD's cluster-based design, at the cost of demanding cross-die performance.
summary.summary: The article examines Intel's Xeon 6 server chiplet design using the AWS r8i instance's Xeon 6 6985P-C, which has 96 Redwood Cove cores, three compute dies, two IO dies, and 480 MB of L3. The author measures cache and memory latency, single-core and chip-level bandwidth, NUMA and cross-die latency and bandwidth, and core-to-core latency under SNC3 mode. Results are compared with Emerald Rapids on AWS i7i and AMD EPYC Turin (9355P), with SPEC CPU2017 single-copy scores also compared against Graviton 4. The closing section discusses the tradeoffs of Intel's logically monolithic mesh versus AMD's two-level interconnect.
